newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Securities Commission wants more power.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Securities Commission wants more power.

text.p: Russia's main securities watchdog, the Federal Commission for the Securities Market, wants more power to protect investors' rights, its Chairman Dmitry Vasilyev said on Wednesday.
"The commission needs more authority," Vasilyev told a news conference. "Crimes on the equities market are becoming more sophisticated."

He said the commission and the Budget Committee of the State Duma lower house of parliament had drafted amendments to the Civil and Criminal Codes making it possible to punish company managers and intermediaries for violating investor rights.
Currently the commission can only reprimand a company which violates investors' rights or withdraw a licence from a market participant, he said.
He said the commission needed the right to fine violators.
"The Central Bank, the Sanitary Inspection, the Fisheries Inspectorate and 20 more ministries have the right to fine," he told a Duma hearing on Tuesday.
"If a fish's rights are violated, violators are punished, but if citizens' rights are violated no one will be be punished because it is considered that we have too many rights."

Vasilyev told the news conference the commission needed the right to carry out investigations, citing a case in March where shares in oil company Surgutneftegaz SNGS.RTS were traded illicitly on the basis of forged receipts.
"Today, tomorrow and in the future the commission will view any event from the point of view of investors' interests," Vasilyev said.
He said Russia lacked a system of class actions.
Vasilyev said investor rights should be the criterion for dividing powers between the Central Bank and his commission.
"Each of us is responsible for different things," he said.

"The Finance Ministry is reponsible for fulfilling the budget, the Central Bank for market and banking system stability and the commission for stock market stability and investors' rights protection. Bank or no bank, an intermediary will die, if the investor does not come to the market with his money."
The commission and the Central Bank have long been at odds over which of them should grant licences for banks' operations on the share market.
